planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; RubyCrisp is a University of Georgia release bred for firmer flesh and thinner, more tender skin than typical muscadines, giving a texture closer to bunch grapes. Build a strong arbor or high-wire trellis to support vigorous vines.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. RubyCrisp is a modern University of Georgia muscadine bred to address the main complaint fresh-market shoppers have about muscadines — thick, tough skin — with noticeably firmer flesh and thinner, more tender skin that make the deep red-to-black berries far more pleasant to eat out of hand, closer to the experience of a bunch grape while keeping the intense, musky-sweet muscadine flavor. Like other muscadines it is naturally resistant to Pierce's disease, downy mildew, and the fungal diseases that plague European wine grapes in the humid South, so home gardeners can grow it without a spray program. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety nearby if RubyCrisp is female-flowered, or check with the nursery on flower type at purchase, since muscadine cultivars vary between self-fertile and female-only. Prune hard in late winter, leaving short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as individual berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Muscadine Grape Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Sterling is a self-fertile bronze muscadine released by NC State University and USDA-ARS in 1981, bred primarily for juice production, and needs a strong arbor or high-wire trellis to support vigorous vines.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. Sterling is a self-fertile bronze muscadine released jointly by North Carolina State University and USDA-ARS, bred with juice production as the primary goal — the berries are consistent, productive, and well suited to pressing, though they are equally good eaten fresh. Being self-fertile, a single vine sets a full crop without a second pollinator variety nearby, simplifying the planting for a home gardener who only has room for one plant. Like other muscadines it shrugs off Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make European grapes difficult in the humid South, needing no regular spray program. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster; a light dropcloth under the vine makes fallen ripe fruit easy to gather during peak harvest.
sources: North Carolina State University — Muscadine Grape Release Documentation

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; James is one of the oldest named muscadine selections still in commerce, a large-fruited bronze cultivar that needs a pollinator variety nearby since it produces only female flowers. Build a strong arbor or high-wire trellis to support vigorous vines.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis, and plant a self-fertile muscadine variety nearby for pollination, since James produces only female flowers. James is one of the oldest named muscadine selections still widely grown, a historic bronze cultivar prized for very large, sweet berries with the classic musky muscadine flavor, harvested for generations across the Deep South for fresh eating, jelly, and wine. Its long track record in Southern gardens speaks to its reliability and adaptability across a range of soils and conditions. Like other muscadines it resists Pierce's disease and the major fungal diseases of the humid South without a spray program. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Pineapple is a self-fertile bronze muscadine noted for a distinctive mild pineapple-like flavor note layered over the classic musky muscadine taste. Build a strong arbor or high-wire trellis to support vigorous vines.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. Pineapple is a self-fertile bronze muscadine grown by home gardeners and small vineyards for its distinctive flavor — a mild, sweet, tropical pineapple note layered over the classic musky muscadine taste, unusual enough among muscadine varieties to have earned the fruit its name. Being self-fertile, one vine sets a full crop without a second pollinator variety planted nearby, making it an easy choice for a single-vine home planting. As with other muscadines, it resists Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make European wine grapes difficult to grow in the humid South, so no regular spray program is needed. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest berries as they ripen and slip easily from the cluster.
